summary: This informational document supplies test vectors for the RC4 stream cipher. Implementers can compare their output to the known values to check correctness. It is not an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A test vector is an answer key. If your code produces the same scrambled output as these examples, it is probably doing the cipher right.

questions: how to verify an rc4 implementation
why discard initial rc4 keystream bytes
is rc4 still safe to use
subtitle: Known-answer keystream outputs that let implementers check whether their RC4 code is correct.

tldr.problem: Implementers of the RC4 stream cipher need known-good outputs to verify their code, for several key lengths and for different positions in the keystream.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists keystream bytes for two keys at key lengths from 40 to 256 bits and at offsets from 0 to 4096 bytes, generated by three separate implementations that agreed.
tldr.outcome: The RFC warns that RC4 output is distinguishable from random and that its use in new specifications is discouraged. The vectors only aid interoperability of existing specifications.

today: RFC 6229 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFCs listed. The text itself says RC4 is recommended against and should not be used in new specifications.

sections.title: Why These Test Vectors Exist
sections.content:
RC4 is a widely used stream cipher that can take different key lengths. Research cited in the RFC suggests that the first parts of its output need to be discarded, so the document gives vectors at several offsets into the stream as well as for several key lengths.

The motivation came from the implementation of RFC 4345. The vectors were collected by generating keystream from three separate implementations, Libgcrypt 1.4.4, Nettle 2.0 and a custom one, and comparing the streams.
sections.plainLanguage: Many people wrote their own RC4 programs, so here is a list of right answers to check against.

sections.title: Keys, Lengths and Offsets
sections.content:
There are two keys. Key 1 is the key byte index starting at one: 0x01, 0x02, 0x03 and so on. Key 2 is made by hashing the string "Internet Engineering Task Force" with SHA-256 and truncating the digest to the needed length, keeping the least significant part.

The key lengths are 40, 56, 64, 80, 128, 192 and 256 bits. The stream offsets are 0, 256, 512, 768, 1024, 1536, 2048, 3072 and 4096 bytes. Offset 1536 matches the recommendation in RFC 4345, and offsets 768 and 3072 match recommendations in the SANS entry cited by the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The answers are given for short keys and long keys, and for different places along the scrambled stream, because the very start of the stream is the weakest part.

sections.title: Reading the Vector Tables
sections.content:
For each key length the RFC gives the key, then lines of 16 keystream bytes at chosen positions, shown in both decimal and hexadecimal. The positions run from 0 up to 4096, and include 16, 240, 256 and 496 and similar spots just before and after each 256-byte boundary.

For example, with the 40-bit key 0x0102030405 the 16 bytes at offset 0 start with b2 39 63 05. An implementation that skips ahead in its keystream and compares against the matching line can check any listed offset.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line says where you are in the stream and what 16 scrambled bytes you should see there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is blunt. RC4 does not meet the basic criteria required for an encryption algorithm, because its output is distinguishable from random. The use of RC4 continues to be recommended against, and its use in new specifications is discouraged.

The document says it is intended only to aid the interoperability of existing specifications that use RC4. It is also meant to be considered a Code Component, available under the Simplified BSD License.
sections.plainLanguage: These answers help old programs keep working, but nobody should build new things with this cipher.
